newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Red Cross killings seen aimed at Chechnya peace.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross killings seen aimed at Chechnya peace.

text.p: Russia and the Chechen rebels denounced the murder of six Western relief workers as they slept at a hospital compound in Chechnya as a provocation aimed at disrupting attempts to bring peace to the rebel region.

The killing of five women and one man from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in the Chechen village of Novye Atagi on Tuesday spurred several other international relief organisations to pull out of Chechnya.

Masked gunmen broke at dawn into a house where the workers were sleeping and shot them dead, apparently with silenced guns. They had been helping to run the hospital in Novye Atagi some 17 km (11 miles) southeast of the regional capital Grozny,
The murdered workers came from Norway, the Netherlands, Canada, Spain and New Zealand.

The ICRC in Geneva named them as: Hans Elkerbout (Netherlands Red Cross), Ingeborg Foss (Norwegian Red Cross), Nancy Malloy (Canadian Red Cross), Gunnhild Myklebust (Norwegian Red Cross) and Sheryl Thayer (New Zealand Red Cross) and Fernanda Calado, a Spanish nurse under contract to the ICRC.
Christophe Hensch, a Swiss man who ran the project, survived but suffered gunshot wounds.
Rebel leaders described the killing as a "political provocation" aimed at ruining the peace process and disrupting local elections but did not say who they blamed.

The Russian Interfax news agency quoted Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin as saying killing was a "cruel and senseless crime" that could destabilise the situation in the region. He also stopped short of pointing the finger at anyone.
Under a deal signed with the rebels on August 31, Moscow is withdrawing forces sent to Chechnya in December 1994 to quell the region's independence drive.
The rebels agreed to put off for five years a decision on the future political status of Chechnya.
Local polls planned for January 27 will elect a new regional leader and parliament. All notable separatist leaders are running for the top post in Chechnya.
Rebel leaders have warned that influential opponents of a peace deal who had profiteered from the war will try to disrupt the elections and undermine peace.

Russian officials have also talked about a sinister "third force" and included in it radical separatist fighters who saw the peace deal as a betrayal by their leaders and have vowed to fight on for the independence.
One such hardliner, field commander Salman Raduyev, seized 21 Russian policemen on Saturday and is defying demands by the separatist leadership to set them free.

President Boris Yeltsin's envoy to Chechnya, Ivan Rybkin, who visited rebel leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev in Grozny on Tuesday, was shown on television saying the polls should go ahead despite provocations.
As the Russians and rebels struggled to keep the situation in the region under control, major international aide agencies started moving out of Chechnya.
The ICRC's Thierry Meyrat told a news conference in Moscow that the agency was pulling out all its international staff, leaving local staff to look after the hospital.

A convoy with coffins carrying the bodies of the Red Cross workers left Grozny on Tuesday for a neighbouring town outside Chechnya and ICRC officials said they would be flown to Moscow in the coming days.

The office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), which has no staff in Chechnya itself, said it had frozen all humanitarian work for 80,000 displaced Chechens in neighbouring areas.
The Paris-based medical charity Medecins du Monde (World Doctors) said it had pulled out of Chechnya and would not return until the January 27 elections.
